items.text:
This passage is doing the concrete work for the essay's fourth and final argument against machine consciousness: it's not just asserting "simulation isn't instantiation" (the abstract claim made just before it), it's showing you what that means with everyday cases, before turning it into a general rule you can apply to consciousness itself.

The move it's answering sits one block earlier. At [spya-fz5xq5] Seth opens this section by noting that Turing-based computers can simulate almost anything, including things that aren't themselves computational — continuous or random processes, say. The worry that follows is: if a computer can simulate a brain in perfect detail, doesn't that mean it has *made* whatever the brain makes, including consciousness? This passage blocks that inference. A simulation of digestion doesn't digest anything, a simulation of a rainstorm doesn't get anything wet, a simulated living creature isn't alive — these are meant as obviously true cases that soften you up for the harder, contested one: a simulated brain isn't conscious, unless consciousness itself turns out to just be an algorithm [spya-npjt4j].

The general rule the passage lands on — a simulation of X only brings X into being if X is itself "a computational process (specifically, an algorithm)" [spya-npjt4j] — is the hinge the whole essay swings on here. It's really a restatement, in sharper form, of "map vs. territory" from the sentence right before it [spya-cepmwf], and it sets up the very next block, where Seth applies it directly: a simulated brain will only be conscious "if consciousness is a matter of computation," which is exactly computational functionalism, the assumption his first three arguments (brain-as-computer, other non-Turing dynamics, biological naturalism) were built to undermine [spya-pbcr03].

One phrase worth flagging: "causal powers and intrinsic properties." The article doesn't spell this out, but that language echoes the philosopher John Searle's Chinese Room argument, where he argued a system could manipulate symbols correctly without those symbols having the actual causal powers of a mind (his slogan was that brains cause minds through their specific biological causal powers, not merely their formal structure) — background knowledge, not something checkable in this piece, but useful for hearing where the vocabulary comes from, and it fits with Seth's own citation of Searle's "biological naturalism" earlier in the essay [spya-hj5y6s].

So reading it again: treat the digestion/rainstorm/life examples as a ladder of increasingly obvious cases meant to make the final, contested case (simulated brain ≠ conscious brain) feel like it belongs on the same rung, not a special exception.
items.context: Computational simulations generally lack the causal powers and intrinsic properties of the things being simulated. A simulation of the digestive system does not actually digest anything. A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet. If we simulate a living creature, we have not created life. In general, a computational simulation of X does not bring X into being — does not instantiate X — unless X is a computational process (specifically, an algorithm) itself. Making the point from the other direction, the fact that X can be simulated computationally does not justify the conclusion that X is itself computational.

items.text:
This passage is the emotional and argumentative peak of Seth's third argument against machine consciousness — "Life Matters" [spya-e7jqx4]. He's been building toward the claim that consciousness may require being alive, not just running the right computation, and here he pushes that claim down to the smallest possible scale: not just organisms, but individual cells and their metabolism.

To follow it, you need two things he set up earlier and is now fusing together. The first is **predictive processing**: the idea that the brain doesn't passively receive sensory data but constantly generates guesses about what's causing its inputs and corrects those guesses when they're wrong — described earlier as the brain "continually explaining away its sensory inputs by updating predictions about their causes" [spya-dp8sem], with conscious experience itself framed as "a kind of controlled hallucination" [spya-xhvztm]. He then extended this to the body itself: predicting and regulating things like heart rate and oxygen levels, because "the primary duty of any brain is to keep its body alive" [spya-b59nm2].

The second is **autopoiesis**, a term he introduced a few sections earlier — "self-production," the fact that even a single living cell is constantly rebuilding the material conditions of its own existence, "regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence" [spya-cf8rt8]. Outside the article, this word comes from the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, who used it to define what makes something alive: a system that continuously produces and repairs the very components that make it up, unlike a machine, which doesn't remake its own parts.

In spya-vys3vj, Seth is arguing these two things are actually one thing. "This drive to stay alive doesn't bottom out anywhere in particular" [spya-vys3vj] means the prediction-and-correction loop he described for brains and bodies isn't a special trick brains do — it goes all the way down into the cell's metabolism, where molecules are constantly being monitored and corrected too. So the "Bayesian best-guessing" (statistical updating of beliefs from evidence, the mathematical machinery behind predictive processing) that explains perception is, he claims, the same kind of process as the self-repairing chemistry that keeps a cell alive [spya-vys3vj]. That's the "mathematical line" he says can be drawn from raw metabolism up to conscious experience.

The stakes of this move: if he's right, consciousness isn't something you could get by running the right algorithm on silicon, because silicon isn't doing this kind of continuous self-production — it directly feeds his conclusion in the next block that "it is life, rather than information processing, that breathes fire into the equations of experience" [spya-pfkhtt]. Worth reading spya-cf8rt8 and spya-b59nm2 again alongside this one if the jump from "cell metabolism" to "consciousness" feels too fast — that's exactly the gap he's trying to bridge.
items.context: This drive to stay alive doesn’t bottom out anywhere in particular. It reaches deep into the interior of each cell, into the molecular furnaces of metabolism. Within these whirls of metabolic activity, the ubiquitous process of prediction error minimization becomes inseparable from the materiality of life itself. A mathematical line can be drawn directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self.
